Executive Overview

Track growth, profitability and the contribution of major business dimensions over time.

Growth qualityMargin mixRegional contribution

Business interpretation

Sales accelerated strongly in 2017, while profit growth lagged revenue growth. This indicates that top-line expansion did not translate proportionally into earnings. Regional and category views help identify where growth is both large and economically productive.

Decision use

Use this view to separate scale from quality of growth: high revenue should be assessed together with profit margin, not in isolation.

Portfolio economics

Product & Market Performance

Compare sub-category economics, product contribution and regional profitability to identify where commercial resources create or destroy value.

Portfolio matrixContribution analysisMargin heatmap
Portfolio analytics
Sub-category profit waterfall

Business interpretation

Technology combines scale with strong profitability, while Furniture is materially less efficient. Tables is the largest sub-category loss contributor at approximately $-17,725. The portfolio view highlights products that generate high revenue but weak or negative margins—priority candidates for pricing, sourcing or assortment review.

Decision use

Prioritize high-sales/high-margin products for growth, investigate high-sales/low-margin products for commercial leakage, and rationalize persistently loss-making items.

Customer value

Customer & Marketing Analytics

Use purchase recency, frequency, spend and profitability to distinguish high-value relationships from margin-risk and low-engagement customers.

RFMCustomer concentrationValue segmentation
RFM segmentation
Customer value map
Customer concentration / Lorenz curve
Customer segmentCustomersMedian recencyMedian ordersMedian salesMedian profitSales share

Marketing interpretation

The customer base separates into distinct value profiles. The Core Value group accounts for the majority of sales and positive profit contribution. The Margin Risk group combines meaningful spend with negative profitability and higher average discount exposure, suggesting that retention activity should be paired with pricing discipline rather than blanket promotional incentives.

Segmentation method

K-means clustering is applied to standardized log-transformed recency, frequency, monetary value and signed profit. The number of clusters is selected from 3–6 using the highest silhouette score; the validated solution uses 3 clusters.

Commercial effectiveness

Pricing & Profitability

Quantify how discount intensity changes margin economics and identify where promotional activity becomes value destructive.

Price-volume tradeoffMargin erosionSegment economics
Pricing analytics
Discount–margin response curve
Segment scale–margin matrix

Business interpretation

Discount levels of 30% and above generated approximately $-135,376 of aggregate loss, equivalent to a -37.3% margin on those sales. The relationship is not simply “more discount equals more volume”: deeper discounts materially deteriorate contribution economics and require tighter product- and segment-specific controls.

Decision use

Use discount thresholds as guardrails, then refine them by sub-category and customer segment. Promotional decisions should be evaluated against contribution margin rather than sales volume alone.

Predictive analytics

Profit Prediction & Model Validation

Estimate transaction-level profit using order economics and business context, with chronological validation to assess performance on future periods rather than random in-sample splits.

Gradient boostingWalk-forward validationFeature importance
Out-of-sample validation
R² 0.772Gradient boosting on 2017 holdout.
MAE $23Average absolute prediction error.
RMSE $115Penalizes large prediction errors.
Linear baseline R² 0.383Nonlinear model materially improves explanatory power.
Model calibration: actual vs predicted profit
Out-of-sample feature importance
Residual density & asymmetry
Walk-forward model stability

Decision interpretation

The predictive model confirms that transaction sales value and discount intensity are the dominant drivers of profit outcomes, followed by sub-category context. Performance varies across holdout years, which is expected in retail data and reinforces the importance of monitoring model stability rather than relying on a single accuracy statistic.

Model design

Gradient boosting with Huber loss is trained on sales, quantity, discount, shipping time, ship mode, customer segment, category, sub-category and region. The primary validation trains on 2014–2016 and tests on 2017. Additional walk-forward tests use 2015, 2016 and 2017 as successive future holdouts.

Data & methodology. Analysis uses the attached Sample Superstore dataset: 9,994 transaction lines from 3 January 2014 to 30 December 2017. Data-quality checks found no missing values, duplicate rows, invalid discount rates, negative sales, or shipping dates preceding order dates. Sales, profit, customer, product, region, category, discount and date fields are aggregated directly from the source records; predictive metrics are calculated on chronological holdout samples.
